analysis.one_liner: Automatically abolishes most domestic federal agencies on a schedule unless Congress votes to save each one.
analysis.headline: Introduced with zero cosponsors in the final two weeks of the session, the bill was referred to committee and died on January 3, 2019 without any vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would put most cabinet departments — Agriculture, Commerce, Education, Energy, Health and Human Services, Housing and Urban Development, Labor, Interior, Transportation, Veterans Affairs, and Treasury offices — on an automatic abolition schedule beginning two years after passage, unless a new federal law saved each one before its date. Agencies not named would also be abolished unless Congress had passed a resolution in the previous ten years disapproving their abolishment, and every surviving agency would face abolition again every ten years. Agency heads would have to file reports justifying their existence a year before their abolition dates.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, the main beneficiaries would be industries and interests that bear the cost of federal regulation and taxes. Abolishing Treasury offices would eliminate the IRS and the agencies under the Financial Services Committee's jurisdiction, such as the SEC; abolishing Labor would end federal wage-and-hour and workplace safety enforcement. The bill does not redirect any functions or cut taxes, so taxpayers would not automatically see savings — the programs would simply end.

how_it_helps.text: It would end federal regulatory and tax enforcement by default: Treasury offices (including the IRS), agencies under the Financial Services Committee's jurisdiction, and the Department of Labor would be abolished on a set schedule unless a new law saved each one, leaving employers and financial firms with no federal wage, safety, or securities enforcement.

It would force a periodic, one-way downsizing of the federal government: every agency that survived would face automatic abolishment again every ten years, and could only be saved by an affirmative act of Congress, not by simply doing nothing.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people who depend on the affected agencies: Medicare and Medicaid patients (HHS), veterans using VA health care, students with federal loans and grants (Education), farmers relying on USDA programs and meat inspection, low-income households receiving food and housing assistance (USDA, HUD), workers protected by Labor Department rules, and travelers (Transportation, including the FAA). Roughly two million federal employees would also lose their jobs, and with the IRS abolished, the government could not collect the taxes that fund whatever remained.
analysis.who_pays_short: Medicare patients, veterans, students, workers, taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Abolishment is the default: an agency dies unless a full law is enacted to save it, so a single chamber's inaction — or a president's veto — would end programs serving millions, with no requirement that anyone deliberate first.

The bill provides no plan for continuing critical functions. It only allows agency heads a year to dispose of assets and liabilities; there is nothing about who would run Medicare payments, food inspections, air traffic control, veterans' hospitals, or tax collection afterward.
The carve-outs are lopsided: the Defense, State, Homeland Security, and Justice departments are exempted, while the agencies delivering benefits and economic oversight are the ones scheduled to die.

Even a supporter would have to concede it is unworkable as written: with the IRS abolished and no replacement, the federal government could not collect revenue to pay for anything that survived, including the exempted Defense Department.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated idea — that Congress should periodically justify agencies — is buried inside a design that requires no judgment at all: abolition happens automatically and saving an agency requires an affirmative law, with no transition for the functions people depend on. The costs fall overwhelmingly on people who rely on Medicare, veterans' care, student aid, food safety, and workplace protections, while the gains flow to interests that want federal regulation and tax enforcement gone. As written, it is a statement bill, not a workable restructuring plan.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the last two weeks of the congressional session and sent to a committee that never acted on it, so it simply died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bradley Byrne introduced the bill on December 19, 2018, the final stretch of the 115th Congress, with no cosponsors.
It was referred the same day to the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, which took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote.
The 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, and the bill expired with it; all federal agencies remain in place.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people who rely on these agencies — Medicare and Medicaid patients, veterans, students, workers, and taxpayers — are better off because the bill never advanced; nothing changed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: People who rely on federal agencies

for.name: Rep. Bradley Byrne
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 19, 2018 and referred it to the Oversight Committee; recruited no cosponsors.

for.name: Conservative groups pushing to shrink the administrative state
for.what_they_did: Promoted agency-sunset proposals of this general design, which this bill mirrored.

against.name: Rep. Trey Gowdy
against.role: Chair, House Oversight and Government Reform Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee received the bill on the day it was introduced and never scheduled it for consideration before the Congress ended.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor in the two weeks between its introduction and the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, and the bill had a single Republican sponsor with zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split was ever measured.

industries.industry: Financial services (banks, securities firms, tax-facing businesses)
industries.note: Abolishing Treasury offices would eliminate the IRS, and agencies whose authorizing bills go to the Financial Services Committee — such as the SEC — would also face automatic abolishment. The industry would gain from lost oversight and lost tax enforcement, costs the public would bear directly.

industries.industry: Regulated employers (wage, safety, and labor law)
industries.note: The Department of Labor was scheduled for abolishment eight years after enactment, ending federal wage-and-hour and workplace safety enforcement. Employers would gain from the removal of rules; workers would bear the cost.

industries.industry: Defense, State, Homeland Security, and Justice departments
industries.note: These departments are explicitly exempted from abolition while every domestic agency is scheduled to die. They would gain budget share and relative standing, though the bill gives them no new powers.

Abolishing the Department of Health and Human Services would end the machinery that pays Medicare and Medicaid claims. Providers and insurers would lose enormous program revenue at the same time beneficiaries lost coverage administration.

The Department of Agriculture was first on the abolishment schedule, two years after enactment. Farmers would lose subsidy, crop insurance, and program delivery, while consumers would lose federal food safety inspection.

Abolishing the Department of Education would end the federal student aid programs the servicing and lending industry administers. The industry would lose its federal business as borrowers lost their aid.
